distillation_scope: Pure disease-name leaf distillation for the full clinical spectrum of Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state. Type 2 diabetes, type 1 diabetes, infection-triggered HHS, medication-triggered HHS, stroke presentations, coma, pediatric HHS, and mixed DKA-HHS physiology are represented only as mechanisms, context axes, risk factors, event hazards, treatment modifiers, or case evidence; they are not part of the disease name.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Relative insulin deficiency with severe insulin resistance
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Insufficient effective insulin action plus stress hormone and insulin-resistance physiology allows marked hyperglycemia while residual insulin action often suppresses substantial ketogenesis.

Infection, stroke, myocardial infarction, pancreatitis, dehydration, medication exposure, surgery, missed treatment, or poor intake increases catecholamines, cortisol, glucagon, and inflammatory stress, amplifying hyperglycemia and fluid loss.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Extreme hyperglycemia from hepatic output and impaired disposal
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Severe insulin resistance and inadequate insulin permit very high glucose concentrations, glucosuria, and osmotic diuresis.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Osmotic diuresis with severe free-water and electrolyte deficit
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Glucosuria causes polyuria, natriuresis, potassium loss, free-water deficit, dehydration, prerenal azotemia, and AKI risk; water loss often exceeds sodium loss and can produce corrected hypernatremia.

High effective osmolality and sodium-water shifts impair cerebral function, causing lethargy, delirium, seizure, coma, focal deficits, and vulnerability to cerebral edema or osmotic demyelination during rapid shifts.

Residual insulin effect usually limits lipolysis and hepatic ketogenesis, so ketones are absent or small and severe ketoacidosis is not the dominant geometry; overlap with DKA is represented by observed ketone and acidosis axes rather than by changing the disease name.
Severe dehydration, hemoconcentration, endothelial dysfunction, inflammation, immobility, and platelet/coagulation activation increase arterial and venous thrombosis risk, including ischemic stroke.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Shock, AKI, rhabdomyolysis, arrhythmia, and multiorgan injury cascade
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Volume depletion, hyperosmolality, hypernatremia, electrolyte shifts, hypoperfusion, infection or trigger illness, rhabdomyolysis, respiratory failure, stroke, and delayed treatment converge on near-term mortality risk.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Controlled recovery with fluids, insulin, electrolytes, and trigger control
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Adequate volume restoration, gradual osmolality correction, potassium-aware insulin, electrolyte monitoring, and precipitant control reverse hyperglycemia and dehydration while avoiding rapid osmotic injury.

mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Inadequate effective insulin action raises hepatic glucose output and impairs peripheral disposal.
Stress hormones and inflammatory triggers worsen hyperglycemia.
Glucosuria creates osmotic diuresis and volume deficit.
Extreme glucose directly contributes to effective hyperosmolality.
Free-water deficit and corrected hypernatremia raise tonicity and neurologic injury risk.
Hemoconcentration and dehydration increase viscosity and thrombosis risk.
Coma, seizure, osmotic brain injury, and stroke pathways worsen organ support needs and mortality risk.
Severe dehydration leads to shock, AKI, rhabdomyolysis, and electrolyte injury.
Extreme hyperglycemia is the central observed expression of HHS.
Many HHS presentations occur after weeks to months of uncontrolled glycemia.
Glucose is a major contributor to effective serum osmolality.
Free-water loss and sodium concentration raise tonicity.
Measured sodium can be low, normal, or high, but severe free-water loss often raises measured sodium.
Corrected sodium exposes true free-water deficit despite translocational effects of glucose.
Total-body potassium deficit is common even when measured potassium is normal or high before insulin.
Osmotic diuresis produces dry mucosa, poor perfusion, and clinical dehydration.
Glucosuria drives polyuria before late volume collapse.
Hyperosmolality and volume loss cause thirst.
Uncontrolled diabetes and fluid loss can cause weight loss.
Prerenal azotemia raises BUN.
Hypovolemia and AKI raise creatinine.
Residual insulin action suppresses substantial ketogenesis.
Blood ketones are absent or small in typical HHS.
Urine ketones are absent or small in typical HHS.
Hypertonicity and dehydration cause lethargy, confusion, obtundation, or delirium.
Severe hyperosmolality may progress to coma.
Seizures can occur with severe hypertonicity, osmotic injury, or comorbid neurologic triggers.
HHS can mimic stroke with focal deficits or coexist with ischemic stroke.
Volume depletion, stress, infection, or shock increases heart rate.
Severe volume depletion can lower perfusion pressure.
Stress leukocytosis or infection can raise WBC.
Fever suggests infection or inflammatory precipitant, while temperature can be normal or low in HHS itself.
Prerenal hypoperfusion, rhabdomyolysis, and trigger illness raise AKI risk.
Severe dehydration and trigger illness can cause shock.
Rapid osmotic shifts or severe pediatric hyperosmolar crises can lead to cerebral edema.
Large or rapid sodium/osmolality shifts can cause pontine or extrapontine osmotic demyelination.
Hyperviscosity and inflammatory stress raise arterial and venous thrombosis hazards.
HHS can create a prothrombotic milieu and may coexist with ischemic stroke.
Hyperosmolality, electrolyte disturbance, dehydration, seizure, and hypoperfusion can precipitate rhabdomyolysis.
Potassium shifts, hypoperfusion, and rapid treatment changes can destabilize cardiac rhythm.
Shock, AKI, coma, stroke, thrombosis, rhabdomyolysis, arrhythmia, and trigger illness converge on death risk.

axes.shape_free_text: Known diabetes mellitus, prior hyperglycemia, diabetes medication exposure, or established diabetic care context.
Presentation suggests newly recognized diabetes with high HbA1c, osmotic prodrome, weight loss, no prior diagnosis, or new insulin requirement.
Clinical or microbiologic context of infection acting as an HHS precipitant; organism identity and source adjudication remain context or confirmatory evidence.
Limited access to water or impaired ability to drink due to frailty, cognitive impairment, institutionalization, isolation, sedation, stroke, vomiting, or dependency.

Recent medication or nutrition context that can worsen hyperglycemia, such as glucocorticoids, atypical antipsychotics, thiazides, sympathomimetics, calcineurin inhibitors, enteral feeds, or parenteral nutrition.
Heart failure, advanced kidney disease, pulmonary edema, ARDS, dialysis dependence, or other context that narrows the safe fluid-resuscitation window.
Serum or plasma glucose, often extremely high in HHS.
Chronic glycemia context; often high in new or uncontrolled diabetes but may be less informative when HHS is acute on a known diabetes background.
Measured, calculated, or effective serum/plasma osmolality. HHS is characterized by high tonicity; reports may provide total or effective osmolality.
Measured sodium; may be low from glucose-driven water shift, normal, or high when free-water loss dominates.
Sodium corrected for hyperglycemia; high values reveal severe free-water deficit and guide osmolality-aware fluid therapy.
Measured potassium can be low, normal, or high despite total-body depletion; insulin and fluids can rapidly lower it.
Chloride is variable at presentation and during saline therapy.
Serum bicarbonate or total CO2; usually normal or mildly low in HHS and lower values indicate DKA overlap, lactic acidosis, renal failure, or another acid-base process.
Arterial or venous pH; usually near normal or mildly acidemic in HHS, while marked acidemia suggests DKA overlap, lactic acidosis, renal failure, shock, or another process.
Anion gap is often normal or mildly elevated in HHS; marked widening points toward DKA overlap, lactate, renal failure, toxins, or rhabdomyolysis context.
Base excess/base deficit; often near normal or mildly negative in HHS unless overlap acidosis is present.
Serum beta-hydroxybutyrate; usually absent or small in HHS, higher values indicate DKA overlap or mixed ketosis.
Semi-quantitative blood ketone positivity; typical HHS has absent or small ketones.
Ketonuria on urine dipstick; typical HHS has absent or small ketonuria, but mixed HHS-DKA may be positive.
BUN rises with dehydration, prerenal azotemia, catabolism, GI bleeding, and AKI.
Creatinine rises with dehydration, AKI, baseline kidney disease, rhabdomyolysis, and shock.
Lactate may be normal or elevated from hypoperfusion, seizure, sepsis, adrenergic stress, or shock.
Creatine kinase can rise with HHS-associated rhabdomyolysis, seizure, immobilization, hypoperfusion, or hyperosmolality.
WBC may rise from stress leukocytosis, infection, pancreatitis, dehydration, or steroid exposure.
CRP is not a core HHS axis but may rise with infection, pancreatitis, or inflammatory triggers.
Polyuria, nocturia, urinary frequency, or osmotic urine loss before volume collapse.
Excessive thirst or increased fluid intake from hyperosmolality and water loss.
Unintentional weight loss from uncontrolled diabetes, catabolism, and fluid loss.
Fatigue, lethargy, weakness, malaise, poor appetite, or reduced energy before or during HHS.
Nausea, vomiting, anorexia, or poor intake during hyperglycemic dehydration or trigger illness.
Dry mucosa, poor skin turgor, delayed capillary refill, weak pulses, oliguria, or clinical volume depletion.
Heart rate increased by dehydration, stress, infection, pain, or shock; may be normal in some elderly or medicated patients.
Respiratory rate may rise with dehydration, acidosis overlap, sepsis, pulmonary trigger, or respiratory compensation.
Systolic pressure may be preserved or low; severe dehydration or trigger illness can cause hypotension.
Perfusion pressure; falls with severe volume depletion, vasodilation, shock, sedatives, or cardiac comorbidity.
Temperature may be normal or low in HHS; fever suggests infection or inflammatory precipitant.
Urine output may be high during osmotic diuresis and then fall with severe hypovolemia or AKI; treatment targets adequate renal perfusion.
Lethargy, drowsiness, confusion, delirium, obtundation, agitation, decreased consciousness, or coma spectrum.
Coma or unresponsiveness from severe HHS physiology, osmotic injury, shock, seizure, or trigger illness.
Observed seizure during severe hyperosmolality, osmotic brain injury, stroke, hyponatremia/hypernatremia, or trigger illness.
Focal neurologic deficit, aphasia, hemiparesis, visual deficit, or stroke-mimic presentation during HHS. Confirmed stroke remains a separate event context.
AKI hazard from hypovolemia, hyperosmolality, rhabdomyolysis, sepsis, nephrotoxins, or baseline kidney disease.
Shock or circulatory collapse hazard from severe hypovolemia, sepsis, pancreatitis, myocardial trigger, sedatives, or arrhythmia.
Arrhythmia hazard from potassium shifts, hypoperfusion, myocardial disease, acid-base overlap, or treatment-related electrolyte changes.
Cerebral edema hazard from severe hyperosmolar crisis or rapid osmotic shifts, particularly in pediatric or mixed HHS-DKA contexts.
Pontine or extrapontine osmotic demyelination hazard from severe or rapidly changing osmolality/sodium during HHS onset or treatment.
Arterial or venous thrombosis hazard from hyperviscosity, dehydration, immobility, inflammation, or baseline vascular risk.

Ischemic stroke hazard during HHS from hyperviscosity, thrombosis, dehydration, atrial fibrillation, atherosclerosis, or trigger illness; confirmed stroke evidence should be handled as event/context rather than disease-name scope.
Clinically important rhabdomyolysis hazard from hyperosmolality, hypernatremia, dehydration, seizure, immobilization, or hypoperfusion.
Hypoglycemia hazard during treatment when insulin exceeds carbohydrate intake, renal clearance is low, or glucose falls faster than planned.

Lifespan outcome hazard for HHS, emerging from coma, severe hyperosmolality, hypernatremia, shock, AKI, thrombosis/stroke, rhabdomyolysis, arrhythmia, trigger illness, frailty, delayed treatment, and treatment-related osmotic injury.

axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: Glucose is a major measured contributor to tonicity.
Corrected sodium captures free-water deficit and contributes to effective osmolality.
Higher tonicity increases risk of lethargy, delirium, obtundation, and coma.
Severe hypertonicity can provoke seizures, but seizures also depend on neurologic comorbidity.
Clinical volume depletion and prerenal azotemia track together.
Severe volume loss can raise creatinine through AKI.
Rising creatinine marks AKI risk and reduced renal reserve.
Hypoperfusion raises lactate, though sepsis or seizure can contribute independently.
Both severe hypokalemia and hyperkalemia can cause arrhythmia during HHS or treatment.
Extreme tonicity and its correction create osmotic brain injury risk.
Extreme corrected sodium and rapid sodium/osmolality shifts increase osmotic demyelination risk.
Severe hyperosmolality can injure muscle and combine with seizure or immobilization.
Marked CK elevation is the main lab correlate of rhabdomyolysis.
Myoglobin and volume depletion increase AKI risk.
Hyperosmolality and dehydration increase viscosity and thrombotic tendency.
Arterial thrombosis can manifest as ischemic stroke.
Shock is a direct death pathway.
AKI worsens electrolyte, volume, and organ-failure risk.
Stroke during HHS increases death and disability risk.
Severe osmotic demyelination can cause coma, respiratory failure, and death.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Heart failure, renal failure, or pulmonary edema narrows the safe resuscitation window.
Profound hypernatremia requires controlled tonicity correction rather than glucose-only targeting.

treatments.context_specific_role: Restores intravascular and extracellular volume, renal perfusion, and gradual tonicity correction; this is a vector-field effect rather than a label.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Insulin shifts potassium intracellularly and can provoke lethal hypokalemia.
Rapid glucose fall can produce large tonicity shifts.
Mixed HHS-DKA requires continued insulin despite osmolality concerns.

treatments.context_specific_role: Lowers glucose and suppresses ongoing hyperglycemic drive after volume and potassium safety are addressed.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Reduced renal clearance changes potassium replacement safety.

treatments.context_specific_role: Keeps potassium and related electrolytes on a safe trajectory while fluids and insulin correct HHS.

sigma_modulation.clinical_rationale: Frequent reassessment and controlled fluid/insulin changes reduce uncontrolled osmotic volatility.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Profound corrected hypernatremia is the main context where osmolality strategy changes treatment vector.
Worsening mental status can reflect ongoing hyperosmolality, cerebral edema, stroke, or osmotic demyelination.

treatments.context_specific_role: Shapes the correction path so glucose, sodium, and osmolality improve without causing rapid osmotic brain injury.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Treating the precipitant reduces counter-regulatory drive only when a real trigger is active.

treatments.context_specific_role: Treats infection, myocardial infarction, stroke, pancreatitis, medication exposure, or other precipitant when that context is observed; agent choice belongs to the precipitant manifold.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Hyperviscosity, immobility, and dehydration increase value of thrombosis prevention.

treatments.context_specific_role: Reduces thrombotic event hazards during the hyperosmolar immobilized state; bleeding contraindications belong to patient context.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Deep coma increases need for airway protection and ICU monitoring.
Severe AKI limits safe fluid/electrolyte/glucose correction.

treatments.context_specific_role: Contains lethal complication vectors while metabolic correction reverses the upstream HHS geometry.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Known diabetes directly raises diabetes-context evidence.
Chronic poor control commonly precedes HHS.
First recognition of diabetes is a real HHS presentation context.
Prodromal osmotic symptoms are common before first diagnosis.
Catabolism and water loss precede diagnosis.
Impaired access to free water permits progressive hyperosmolar dehydration.
Limited drinking capacity worsens free-water deficit.
Frailty and baseline neurologic vulnerability amplify encephalopathy.
Older age, frailty, and reduced reserve increase HHS mortality.
Observed infection or acute illness raises trigger context.
Stress hormones worsen hyperglycemia.
Infection adds leukocytosis to stress leukocytosis.
Sepsis or myocardial/pancreatic triggers can add shock physiology.

treatment_effect_modulation.trigger_control_for_infection_or_intercu: stronger when a real precipitant is active

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Observed medication or nutrition exposure directly raises this context axis.
Glucocorticoids, antipsychotics, thiazides, TPN, or enteral carbohydrate load can worsen hyperglycemia.
Baseline kidney disease raises creatinine background.
Reduced renal excretion changes potassium expression and treatment safety.
Lower renal reserve raises AKI risk.
Advanced CKD narrows fluid safety margin.
Heart failure limits large-volume correction.
Fluid treatment is harder when pulmonary edema or heart failure limits volume restoration.
Pediatric HHS can be a first presentation of diabetes.
Children and adolescents are more vulnerable to cerebral edema during hyperglycemic crisis treatment.

supportive_care: Track HHS by tonicity and perfusion, not glucose alone: serum glucose, measured/effective osmolality, corrected sodium, mental status, dehydration, BUN/creatinine, and urine output should move coherently.

Do not exclude HHS because ketones, bicarbonate, or anion gap are mildly abnormal; mixed DKA-HHS is represented by observed ketosis/acidosis axes or a future combo/subtype, not by changing this leaf name.

Do not absorb sepsis, pancreatitis, stroke, myocardial infarction, medication exposure, or dehydration-only states into the disease name; they remain triggers, mimics, context axes, event hazards, or separate manifolds.

Culture species, final precipitant adjudication, MRI stroke or osmotic demyelination confirmation, diabetes autoantibodies, treatment response, and outcome should stay confirmatory/non-ranking unless the workflow explicitly uses post-workup evidence.

Treatment should enter through vector effects on volume, glucose, sodium/osmolality, electrolytes, thrombosis, neurologic injury, AKI, and trigger context rather than through clinical-ordering labels.
